extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of social psychology, political sociology, and rhetoric; anyone studying crowd behaviour and leadership
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles describing who becomes a leader of crowds, how leaders act, and the main persuasive mechanisms (affirmation, repetition, contagion, prestige) by which opinions and behaviours spread in crowds. Useful for analyzing or producing persuasive group leadership or propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders supply will and organisation to crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as a certain number of living beings are gathered together ... they place themselves instinctively under the authority of a chief. His will is the nucleus around which the opinions of the crowd are grouped and attain to identity. He constitutes the first element towards the organisation of heterogeneous crowds, and paves the way for their organisation in sects; in the meantime he directs them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders turn a collectivity into a cohesive force; a crowd is 'a servile flock that is incapable of ever doing without a master.' The leader's role is organisational as well as persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders often emerge from the led (hypnotised apostles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The leader has most often started as one of the led. He has himself been hypnotised by the idea, whose apostle he has since become. It has taken possession of him to such a degree that everything outside it vanishes, and that every contrary opinion appears to him an error or a superstition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective leaders frequently are converts who become zealots for an idea (example: Robespierre). Their own prior hypnotisation by the idea makes them powerful advocates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological profile of many effective leaders: men of action
rubrics_metrics.description: The leaders we speak of are more frequently men of action than thinkers. They are not gifted with keen foresight... They are especially recruited from the ranks of those morbidly nervous, excitable, half-deranged persons who are bordering on madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits include intense conviction, readiness to sacrifice personal interest, and sometimes near-martyrdom. Such inner certainty imparts great suggestive power to their words and attracts crowds who 'lose all force of will' and turn to those possessing strong-willed qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical opportunists versus true apostles (durability of influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: These leaders are often subtle rhetoricians, seeking only their own personal interest, and endeavouring to persuade by flattering base instincts. The influence they can assert in this manner may be very great, but it is always ephemeral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between leaders who flatter and seek personal gain (short-lived influence) and those animated by genuine creed (longer-lasting, faith-based influence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to arouse faith as central to leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The arousing of faith—whether religious, political, or social, whether faith in a work, in a person, or an idea—has always been the function of the great leaders of crowds, and it is on this account that their influence is always very great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faith multiplies strength ('To endow a man with faith is to multiply his strength tenfold'). Great leaders create faith rather than merely argue logically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders exercise despotic authority and satisfy crowds' need for servitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The leaders of crowds wield a very despotic authority ... They fix the hours of labour and the rate of wages, and they decree strikes, which are begun and ended at the hour they ordain. It is the need not of liberty but of servitude that is always predominant in the soul of crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders can command concrete collective actions; removing leaders often collapses movements (example: arrest of two leaders ended a Paris omnibus strike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders may usurp public authority when official power is weakened
rubrics_metrics.description: At the present day these leaders and agitators tend more and more to usurp the place of the public authorities in proportion as the latter allow themselves to be called in question and shorn of their strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political or institutional weakness creates opportunity for leaders to substitute their authority for that of official institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two classes of leaders by will: intermittent energy vs enduring will
rubrics_metrics.description: Ringleaders and agitators may be divided into two clearly defined classes... one includes the men who are energetic and possess, but only intermittently, much strength of will... the other the men, far rarer, whose strength of will is enduring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermittent-energy leaders (e.g., Ney, Murat, Garibaldi) are useful for sudden daring acts but their energy is transitory. Leaders of enduring will (e.g., St. Paul, Mahomet, Columbus, de Lesseps) have sustained influence and can found lasting movements or institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience as primary means to establish truth among the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience constitutes almost the only effective process by which a truth may be solidly established in the mind of the masses... it is necessary that the experience should take place on a very large scale, and be very frequently repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations to crowds are slow and costly (examples: French Revolution, wars to disabuse beliefs about armies, long periods to show Protectionism harms nations). Historical facts cited to prove points are often ineffective for new generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning is ineffective on crowds; persuasion must appeal to sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are not to be influenced by reasoning, and can only comprehend rough-and-ready associations of ideas... The orators who know how to make an impression upon them always appeal in consequence to their sentiments and never to their reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical chains and prepared speeches often fail; orators must divine and appeal to current sentiments, vary language according to immediate effect (example: speech calming a mob by emotional concession rather than logical refutation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmation as a persuasive device
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirmation pure and simple, kept free of all reasoning and all proof, is one of the surest means of making an idea enter the mind of crowds. The conciser an affirmation is, the more destitute of every appearance of proof and demonstration, the more weight it carries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in religious books, legal codes, political rhetoric, and advertising. Affirmation should be concise and appear unquestionable to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition embeds assertion and builds apparent truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirmation, however, has no real influence unless it be constantly repeated, and so far as possible in the same terms... The thing affirmed comes by repetition to fix itself in the mind in such a way that it is accepted in the end as a demonstrated truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated statements become embedded in unconscious regions; examples include advertising claims and repeated press characterisations that become accepted as truth. Repetition and unanimity can counteract opposing repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contagion (and imitation) spreads ideas, emotions, and behaviours
rubrics_metrics.description: When an affirmation has been sufficiently repeated and there is unanimity in this repetition ... what is called a current of opinion is formed and the powerful mechanism of contagion intervenes. Ideas, sentiments, emotions, and beliefs possess in crowds a contagious power as intense as that of microbes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contagion can act locally or at a distance, spread from lower to higher social classes, and makes imitation effective. For contagion to operate, ideas must be easy to imitate and the crowd's mind must be prepared by prior factors; imitation is an effect of contagion, not a separate mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitability requirement: ideas must not be too different from received opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is needful however, that these individualities should not be in too pronounced disagreement with received ideas. Were they so, to imitate them would be too difficult and their influence would be nil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovations that are too far removed from prevailing beliefs rarely spread; 'men who are too superior to their epoch are generally without influence upon it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige paralyses critical faculty and enforces authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige in reality is a sort of domination exercised on our mind by an individual, a work, or an idea. This domination entirely paralyses our critical faculty, and fills our soul with astonishment and respect... The special characteristic of prestige is to prevent us seeing things as they are and to entirely paralyse our judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige can derive from accumulated repetition (acquired prestige) or from individual qualities (personal prestige). It is the 'mainspring of all authority' and explains why certain works, persons, or monuments are exempt from ordinary criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired (artificial) prestige: titles, rank, robes, uniforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquired prestige is that resulting from name, fortune, and reputation... The mere fact that an individual occupies a certain position, possesses a certain fortune, or bears certain titles, endows him with prestige, however slight his own personal worth. A soldier in uniform, a judge in his robes, always enjoys prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artifacts of status (titles, decorations, uniforms, robes) confer authority even on the unworthy. Cultural examples (peerage in England, judge's robes, uniforms) illustrate how artificial prestige shapes crowd reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal prestige distinct from acquired prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal prestige, on the contrary, is something essentially peculiar to the individual; it may coexist with reputation, glory, and fortune, or be strengthened by them, but it is perfectly capable of existing in their absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal prestige derives from qualities intrinsic to the individual (to be elaborated further in the text). It can exist without titles or wealth and often underpins the most durable forms of leadership.
